about: The words of the chain wreckers (cards: encounters/chain_wreckers_793.json; page: Design/content/chains/wreckers.md). A fire on the wrong sand south of the Canche, 812 and after; the custom of the strand; the abbess of Thanet's lost ship. Titles, what is seen, what is said, the choices, what comes of each (out_...), the news the chain posts, and one art.<card id> line for each card's picture. People speak plainly and name days by feasts. A draft for the user to overwrite. Written 6 Oct 2026.

entries.text: A man on a hatch board
Two fishermen are carrying a man up the bank on a hatch board. He is alive, blue to the lips, and he will not let go of the board.
We took him off the north point at first light. He had walked the sand all night with that board under his arm. He says he is a steersman. He was steering something.

Hunfrith. I had the steering oar of the abbess's ship, of Thanet. Lead and cloth for this river, and six for Rome who paid their passage. Ealdred was master. He is on the banks now with the lead on top of him.

We had the emperor's fire behind us and lost it in the murk, as you do. Then a fire ahead, low. Ealdred said it was the monks on the saint's hill, burning furze for us. The river is north of the saint's hill. So he put her north of the fire.
It was not the hill. It was two leagues south of the hill, on the bare sand. North of that fire there is no river. There are the banks.
He should say that more quietly on this bank.
Have him carried to the guest hall at Saint Josse, and hear all of it
Give him your second cloak and eight pennies, and hear all of it
Ask the fishermen first what they make of it
A wreck is a wreck. Go about your trade

The brothers put him by the fire with a bowl of pulses and he tells it twice, the same both times, which is how you know a true account from a good one. Nine in the crew and six pilgrims. He saw three men wade ashore to the south, toward the fire. He went north, away from it, and cannot say why.

He puts the cloak on over the wet and counts the pennies without meaning to, like any steersman. Then he tells it: nine in the crew, six for Rome, a fire on the wrong sand. Three men went ashore to the south. He says he will not forget the cloak, and seamen say that less often than landsmen do.
Gundbert looks at the river for a while. He says the alehouse is a better place for that question than the bank, and that he will be there after the tide.
They carry him on up the bank. By evening the long street knows that English cloth will be cheap this month, and nobody says why.
The custom of the strand
Gundbert the fisherman has the end of the bench nearest the door. He talks into his cup, so that it could be said afterwards he was talking to the ale.
What the sea lays on the sand is the lord's. That is not a law anyone made. It is like the tide. A third to the people who find it and carry it up, two parts to the hall.
Men too, if nobody on that shore speaks for them. A stranger on a strand has no kin and no lord. He has his keep to pay, and the keep is counted by the one who feeds him.
The Englishman's ship is the third on those banks since the saint's fire first had a brother. Before that, one in ten years.

It began after the wet summer, when the corn rotted standing and the cattle died. That winter the south sand ate lead and cloth and Rhine wine, and nobody there buried a child. I do not say more than that.

A Breton pedlar walked the south sand at night last year asking who kept the fire. He was found in the next river with his pack still on him. Nothing was taken. That is how you are meant to know it was not thieves.
Fill his cup and ask how the banks lie south of the river
Ask who holds the south strand
You have heard enough. Thank him

He draws it in spilt ale. Three banks like the fingers of a hand laid on the table, and between the second and third a gut with two fathoms in it at half tide. 'A boat your size can lie in there all night and be thought a seal. Nothing bigger can. Do not tell me why you asked.'

'Odalric. The emperor's vassal, for his service, from the river to the next river. He is at the palace half the year and knows nothing. His steward Adalwin is on the sand before the gulls are and knows everything. Ask the one what the other knows and you will have two answers and both sworn.'
He nods to the cup. On your way out the woman of the house says, to nobody, that Gundbert has a brother on the south sand and has not spoken to him in two winters.
The evening ebb
You can drop down the river on the evening ebb and lie off the south sand for a night. Hunfrith asks to come. He says he would like to see it from a ship that is not sinking.

North, there. A hand above the water, steady, a little red. That is the emperor's fire at Bononia. It does not move and it does not flicker much. A man can trust it for exactly as long as he can see it.
Now the murk comes off the land and it is gone. This is the hour. A master counts in his head and looks for the next thing he knows.

And there. Low, on the sand, where there is no hill and no house. It burns bright and then dull, the way a fire does when it is fed with something wet. I thought so that night and said nothing, because he was the master.
The old man's gut should open under us about here. If he drew it right.
Anchor well off and watch it till dawn
Creep in with the lead and fix which dune it burns on
Lie in the gut between the banks, close enough to count the men
It is a fire on a beach. Stay in the river

It burns till the tide turns and then somebody lets it die. No ship comes. At first light there is a smear of smoke on the dunes and, north of it, the ribs of the abbess's ship standing out of the sand with carts round her like flies. You have seen the fire. You could not swear to the dune.

Three fathoms, two, two, and the fire comes clear: an iron pan on legs, set on the seaward face of the third dune south of a wreck-post, and a man beside it with a shovel. You have it lined up with a notch in the dunes behind. You could find it again blind, and you could say where it is on oath.

Two fathoms, then the keel is on sand with the ebb still running. You spend the night aground on the outer bank with the fire looking at you, and float off at dawn, wet and bruised and seen. You have seen the fire. So has the fire seen you.

Gundbert drew it right. You lie in two fathoms with a bank on either hand and the fire a long bowshot off: an iron pan on legs on the third dune south of a wreck-post, one old man with a shovel, and a child asleep under a hide. Nobody else. Whoever profits by it is in his bed.
Hunfrith says nothing. He goes back to Saint Josse and sits where he can see the river mouth.
The south sand

At low water the abbess's ship lies on her side a bowshot from the dunes with her planks sprung. Women and children carry bolts of wet cloth up the sand. A man with a bundle of tally sticks stands by an ox cart and cuts a notch for every load.
Adalwin. I keep this strand for Odalric, who holds it of the emperor. You are a trader, by the boat. Good. Then you know what a thing is worth wet.
Everything you see is my lord's by the right of the strand, less the third that goes to those who carry it. I count the two parts. They count the third, and I count it after them.
Three of her men are at the hall, warm and fed, which is more than the sea offered them. Their keep is running. The rest we buried above the tide mark, with a priest. Ask anyone.
It is good cloth. It was good cloth last time. My children have English cloaks now and I pray for whoever wove them.

Fire? The salt pans. People boil brine on this sand when the weather is thick, because thick weather is no use for anything else. If a shipmaster cannot tell a salt pan from Saint Josse, that is a matter between him and his steersman.
Walk round the wreck and look at what is hers
Buy from the steward's cart: six bolts of cloth and two pigs of lead for 60 pennies
Carry a bolt up the sand for the woman, and ask her who keeps the fire

The lead is still in her, forty pigs under the sand, and every pig has a small cross cut in its upper face with a chisel: the minster's. So has the one on the steward's cart. He sees you look and turns it over with his foot. You have seen it both ways up.

Less than half their worth, weighed and paid before witnesses, which on this sand means before the people who carried it. Adalwin cuts a notch for you too. 'Now you have bought of my lord in the open, by day. Remember that you did.' The lead has a small cross cut in it. You are a man who owns that now.

She lets you carry it. 'Old Ragenulf boils salt on the third dune. He boiled it there before any ship came to it. The first one was God's doing, or the master's. After that the steward told him which nights the salt needed boiling.' She takes the bolt back. 'He does not sleep. Ask him yourself, he would thank you for it.'
The lord of the strand
Odalric's hall stands behind the dunes among wind-bent thorn, with a new roof. He has you in at once, and sends for ale, and for the three Englishmen from the byre so that you can see they are whole.
You have come about my guests. Look at them. Fed, dry, a blanket each. I found them naked on my sand and I have had them three weeks. I am told I have a kind heart. It is expensive.
Fifty pennies a head covers their keep and the burying of the others. I do not sell Christians. I am owed for bread. There is a difference, and the emperor's judges know it as well as I do.
I can keep them till Martinmas. After that I cannot feed idle men through a winter, and a dealer comes by on the Amiens road who finds work for such people a long way from the sea.
Eadhelm, of the minster's ship. That is Sigehere, and the boy is Wiga. We ask for nothing but that somebody tells the lady abbess we are above ground.
I light no fires. I am at the palace from Easter to harvest. My people boil salt. If you want to know what my people do at night, you have more leisure than I have.
Pay their keep now: 150 pennies for the three
Give your word to carry the news to their abbess and come back before Martinmas
Ask him by what right, and about the fire on his sand

He has the silver weighed and says it is a pleasure to deal with a man who does not argue about bread. The three walk out of the yard behind you in borrowed shoes. At the first dune the boy starts to run and Eadhelm catches him by the hood. 'Walk. We are guests leaving.'

Odalric says a merchant's word is as good as silver until Martinmas and not a day longer. Eadhelm tells you where to find the lady: at the ship-house at Serrae, or wherever her ships are being counted. The boy asks if you could bring his mother's answer too.

'By the right my father's lord had and his before him. The sea is God's and what it puts down is the land's.' He is not angry. He has given the answer before. About the fire he says what the steward said, in nearly the same words, which tells you who taught whom.
The abbess's ship
In the ship-house at Serrae there are rollers on the floor and no ship on them. The abbess stands where the stem would be. A nun with a wax tablet stands half a pace behind her.
The lady asks: how many living, and their names. Then the lead. Then how you come to know.

My house has had ships free of the king's toll since King Aethelbald's day. The charter says: if she is broken, or worn out with great age, or lost by wreck. Whoever wrote it had seen all three. It does not say: or steered on to a sand by a fire.

When King Offa was alive, King Charles wrote to him that our merchants should have his protection in his kingdom, and that if they were wronged they might go to him or to his judges. Both kings are dead. The letter is not. I have had it copied twice.
The archbishop would be glad to hear I had lost a ship and done nothing. He keeps a list of such things.
The lady has been told that our cloth was sold from a cart on that sand. She does not ask who bought it. She notices who offers to say.
Take her silver for the men's keep, and her sealed complaint for the emperor's judges
Take the sealed complaint and leave her silver in her chest till the men stand here
Say what you bought on the sand, and lay it at her feet

The nun counts out a hundred and eighty pennies, fifty a head and thirty for your wind. The abbess seals a leaf: her complaint, the charter's words and King Charles's. 'The emperor's judges sit at the wic after the feast. Forty days; the toll clerk will know the day. You are my mouth there. Try to be a short one.'

The nun stops counting. The abbess looks at you for the first time. 'Then the minster will owe you. I dislike that less than I expected.' She seals the leaf, and has the nun write an order for four casks of Rhine wine for the altar, at a price a Frisian would be ashamed to ask.

Six bolts and two pigs of lead on the ship-house floor. The nun turns a pig over and finds the cross. The abbess says: 'You bought it in the open, by day, of a man who had it by custom. No court would touch you. And you brought it across the sea to me.' She has your sixty pennies added to the hundred and eighty, and the pig with the cross goes in with the sealed leaf, as a witness that cannot be frightened.
The byre
The three Englishmen are mucking out Odalric's byre. They have been given work, so that it can be said they were given work. The boy has a cough.
The merchant, and before Martinmas. I told my steward you would come. He had a penny on it that you would not.
A hundred and fifty, as we said. I have not added the weeks since, though bread did not stop being eaten.
Master. Whatever you do in there, know this first: the carts were on the sand before we struck. I saw the oxen by the fire's light. Nobody yokes oxen at midnight to boil salt.

I hear a sealed leaf has come over the sea. I have stood before judges with twelve good men at my side who will swear what I swear. How many will swear for you on this shore? Count them on the way home.
Pay the hundred and fifty
Offer a hundred, and argue the rest
Pay nothing yet. Tell him that free men in a byre are a thing judges ask about
Weighed, counted, and a cup of ale on it. The three walk out behind you. Eadhelm does not look back at the byre. Sigehere does, and spits, and Eadhelm tells him to save it for the sea.

You say that three weeks' bread for three men is not fifty pennies a head on any coast you have traded, and that the boy has been worked. Odalric laughs and takes a hundred. 'I am told Frisians count the holes in a net and pay for the string.' The men walk out with you.

He hears you out, takes the hundred, and has the steward cut a tally for seventy more, twenty of it for the insult. 'Your half of the stick. Mine stays here. I shall know where you are when I want it.' The men walk out with you. You owe a lord seventy pennies on a split stick.

Odalric says that is a brave thing to say in a man's own yard and that he will remember the day. Eadhelm, behind him, nods to you once: go on. The boy coughs. Nobody goes with the dealer before Martinmas; that much was promised before witnesses.
What they saw

At Saint Josse the four Englishmen sit along the south wall of the guest hall in the sun, the three from the byre and Hunfrith. They have been comparing what each of them saw, the way a crew does after a bad night.
The carts were on the sand before we struck. Oxen yoked, by the fire. That is not finding. That is waiting.
And the fire was fed with pitch. I smelt it over the water and took it for our own seams. Furze does not smell like that, and brine does not need it.
Ealdred was a careful master. I want that said somewhere it will be heard. He steered for a thing he knew, and somebody had made him a second one.
It is written: cursed be he who makes the blind man lose his way. A master in the murk is a blind man. I have said so to people of that shore in confession, and I may not tell you what they answered.
The boy has a riddle for you, for the bread. It is the one about the thing that fights the wind and the wave and holds fast when it is let alone. Every boy has it. Let him think he is the first.
Take the three home to Serrae in your own boat
Send the three home by the next Kentish keel, and take Hunfrith at your steering oar
Ask all four to wait here and swear to it before the emperor's judges

They come aboard with nothing to stow. Eadhelm takes a rope without being asked and Sigehere finds the bailer. By the time the chalk is in sight you have a good deal more English than you sailed with, most of it about weather. Hunfrith stays: he says he will wait at Saint Josse till the fire is out, one way or another.

Hunfrith says he has no ship, no master, and a lady who will ask him why he is alive. A Frisian boat is small, but it floats. He knows the Kentish sands from the Wantsum to the Dour and now, he says, one more sand than he wanted. The other three sail on a Fordwic keel two days later with a letter from the guest-master.

Eadhelm asks whether a foreign seaman's oath is worth anything in a Frankish court. The guest-master says it is worth what the men who stand beside him are worth, and that he will find out how many of the wic are willing to stand. They will wait. The boy wants to know if he must swear too. 'You must tell the truth,' says Eadhelm. 'It is the same thing, done slower.'
The salt-boiler

After dark a girl of nine or ten finds you on the bank and says her grandfather is behind the boat sheds and will not come nearer the houses. He is an old man with burnt forearms and salt in the cracks of his hands.
Ragenulf. I boil salt on the third dune. I have boiled it there since before your beard. You know what else I do or you would not have come round the sheds.

The first ship was nobody's doing. I was boiling late. She came in on my pan like a moth. In the morning there was wine on the sand, and it was the winter the children were eating bark. I thanked God for it. I did.
Then the steward came and said: on thick nights your salt wants boiling on the seaward face, old man, and it wants pitch. He did not say why. He has never said why. He sends pitch.
The brother at Saint Josse will not loose me while it burns. I have not had the Body of the Lord in two Easters. I am old. I count Easters now.
The steward has sent pitch again. Rhine ships are looked for at the wic, Frisians, deep with wine. The next thick night I am to boil. I am telling you because you carried the Englishman up the bank.
Tell him to do as he is told. You will be out there in the gut, between his fire and the ships
Give him thirty pennies for the winter's bread, and ask him to leave the pan cold
Tell him to boil his salt, and say you will be on the sand in the morning with silver
Not tonight. Tell the girl you will think on it
He nods. 'Then if they hang me they hang me for boiling salt, which is my trade.' The girl will come to the bank at dusk on the night. You are to be at sea before the murk.

He holds the silver as if it were hot. 'A cold pan on a thick night. Adalwin will know by midnight.' He will do it. He says you had better be out there all the same, because the steward has hands of his own and knows where the pitch is kept. And he says that if the judges ever ask, he will tell them who sent it.

He looks at you a long while. 'So. I took you for the other kind.' He goes. Four nights later the murk comes down, and in the morning a Frisian ship is on the second bank with her back broken. You buy three casks off Adalwin's cart for the price of one. Your crew stow them without talking. Nobody mentions how many Frisians came ashore.
The old man is gone from behind the sheds when you look again. The girl says he walks back along the sand in the dark and knows every step of it.
The second ship

The murk came down at dusk, as the girl said it would. You are off the south sand with the tower's fire gone. A fire is burning on the dunes. To seaward, a big hull under a reefed sail is standing in for it, deep in the water.
Frisian by her sail. Deep. That is wine, and a master who has done this run before and thinks he knows where he is.
The old man's pan, on the third dune, burning dirty. He has done as he was told.
The third dune is black. The old man kept his word. That fire is north of it, on the beach itself, and it is burning clean pitch. The steward has lit his own.
She has the length of a psalm before she is on the outer bank. If we show a light she may take us for a third lie. If we do not, she is the fourth ship.
Hold your place in the gut, burn a pitch torch at the masthead and wave her off to seaward
Run down across her bows with a torch and hail her
Anchor in deep water and stand by to take her men off
Let her strike, and be first on the sand in the morning

A light where no light should be, lower than the fire and moving: a careful master does not understand it, and what he does not understand he stands away from. She comes round with her sail slatting, a ship's length from the bank, and you lead her out by the gut's mouth with the torch. At dawn a Frisian the size of a door leans over her rail. 'Liudbrand, of Dorestat. I had that fire for Saint Josse. I had it for Saint Josse.' He sends over two casks and a purse, and says the rest he will say at the wic, before people.

She sees the torch late and puts her helm the wrong way. She takes the outer bank beam on and the mast goes. You work the gut in the dark and take nine men off her quarter two at a time before the tide leaves her, with your own boat pounding. At dawn the carts are on the sand, and nine Frisians are standing in your boat watching them.

You cross her bows close enough to see the lead-line in a man's hand and shout the one word every tongue on this sea has for it: sand. She comes round. At dawn her master leans over the rail, a Frisian the size of a door. 'Liudbrand, of Dorestat. I had that fire for Saint Josse.' Two casks and a purse come over, and the rest, he says, at the wic, before people.

You cross her bows and shout, and she holds on: a small boat with a torch, off a strange shore, at night. Then she strikes. You lose skin and an oar getting alongside, and take nine men off her before the tide leaves her. At dawn the carts are on the sand, and nine Frisians are standing in your boat watching them.

She strikes the outer bank a little after midnight. You hear it. At first light you are alongside before the carts are, and nine men come down a rope into your boat. Her master is the last. He looks at the fire, then at the sand, then at you. 'Liudbrand, of Dorestat. You were lying here. You knew.' You tell him what you knew. He is quiet for some time. 'Then we will talk at the wic.'

She strikes a little after midnight. In the morning you are on the sand before Adalwin's carts, and he laughs out loud when he sees whose boat it is. Four casks for the price of one, 'for a man who rises early'. Your steersman stows them and does not look at you for two days. How many of the Frisians came ashore you do not ask.
The emperor's judges

The emperor's two judges, an abbot and a count, sit on a bench before Saint Peter's with the men of the wic standing round. Odalric is there in his good cloak with twelve neighbours behind him. The toll clerk has the abbess's leaf open and is waiting to be told to read.

The complaint of Cwenthryth, abbess, by her seal. A ship of her minster lost on the strand south of this river. Three of her men held for payment. Her goods carried off. And the words of the lord King Charles to King Offa: that their merchants have our protection, and if wronged may come to us or to our judges.

I took what the sea put on my land, as my lord's father did. I fed three naked men and asked the price of bread. The fire is a salt pan. I will swear it, and here are twelve who will swear I am a man to be believed.

Twelve. And for the abbess, a Frisian with a leaf. The emperor sent us to do right by churches, widows, orphans and strangers, and he did not say it would be easy. Merchant: who stands with you, and what have you seen with your own eyes?
If it comes to it we can put the neighbours on oath ourselves and ask them what burns on that sand. They will say salt. Neighbours do, until somebody they fear less than their lord stands up first.
Call them: the Frisian master whose ship you turned, the English seamen, and the proof of the fire
Lay the abbess's leaf and your own oath before them, and let them weigh it
Not at this sitting. You have not the oaths yet

Liudbrand swears first, in Frisian, with his whole crew behind him, and it takes some time because there are nine of them and the judge lets every man speak. Then the Englishmen: the oxen yoked at midnight, the smell of pitch. Then what you saw. The count asks Odalric's twelve whether any of them will swear that carts wait on that sand by chance. Nobody does. The judgement: the men were never owed for; the worth of the lead and the cloth to the abbess, and a third of it to the one who brought the suit, 'since thirds are the custom of that strand'. No fire on that shore by night from this day but one, on the saint's hill, kept by the brothers at Odalric's cost, under the emperor's ban of sixty shillings. And the stranger who brought it is under the emperor's own protection, 'since he will need it'. Odalric bows to the judges and does not look at you at all.

You say what you saw and swear to it alone. The abbot asks Odalric whether he will swear that he never took silver for a Christian man. Odalric considers the abbot, and the emperor behind the abbot, and says he would rather make the lady a gift. The men go free without payment; the worth of the lead is paid, and the judges give you a share of it and the emperor's word over your head for bringing a stranger's wrong to them. Nothing is said about the fire. Nothing was proved about it.

You swear alone. Odalric swears with twelve. The count says, not unkindly, that one oath does not outweigh thirteen, and that a salt pan is a salt pan until somebody shows him otherwise. The suit falls. You pay the clerk thirty pennies for the bench. Odalric says, passing, that his table is still open to a man who knows the price of things. The abbess, the skippers and the sand are all still where they were.
The clerk folds the leaf. The judges go on to a quarrel about a mill. They will sit here again in two months, he says, or their successors will; the emperor's justice comes round like the herring.
The ship in her place

The three seamen are home: the boy's mother has him by the ear on the strand and will not let go. In the ship-house the rollers are still empty. The abbess has the old charter out of its box, which the nun says she has not done since the archbishop last asked to see it.
Three men out of nine, and six pilgrims who will see Rome from a better place than this. I have had Masses said. Now the living.
The king's word is that when a ship of mine is lost by wreck, another may stand in her place, free of his toll as she was. It does not say I must build her. It says: another.
The lady knows the ransom came out of your own chest. That is counted first, and separately.
The lady hears that the lord of that sand holds half a stick with your name on it. She says a debt to such a man is paid quickly or not at all, and she would choose quickly.
And the fire burns still. Yes. I am an abbess, not the emperor. I get my men home and I count what is left. That is what there is.
Let your own keel be the ship in her place, free of toll on this strand
Ask for the mastering of the ship she will build, and the right to one like her
Ask nothing. They were seamen on a sand
Not yet. There is still the fire

She has it said on the strand before the toll man and two witnesses: the Frisian's boat is the minster's ship from this day, in the place of the one lost by wreck, and passes free as she did. The toll man repeats it in the voice of a man learning a psalm he dislikes. The nun counts out six hundred and fifty pennies in three bags. On the far shore the fire burns on thick nights, as it did, and masters who know of it stand further off, and those who do not, do not.

'You want oak, then, not parchment.' She is having a coaster laid down on the strand before winter, ten ells longer than your boat, and the wright is to build a second on the same moulds for whoever the minster names. She names you. Six hundred pennies besides. Hunfrith's cousin is cutting the keel scarf already and says it will be a better ship than the last, 'which is not what one says to an abbess'.

The nun writes nothing for a moment, which in her is astonishment. The abbess says that Mercians do not leave a debt lying where the archbishop might find it. Your boat is named the ship in the lost one's place whether you like it or not. Twenty bolts of the minster's cloth come down to the strand on a sledge, and three hundred pennies 'for the wind'. The boy's mother brings a cheese and will not be refused either.
The abbess puts the charter back in its box herself. 'Then come when it is out, or when you are tired. Either is an answer.'
Help in shipwreck
The alehouse is full of shipmasters, Frisian at one end and English at the other, and for once they are sitting at one table. Liudbrand has a small oak box in front of him with nothing in it yet.

This man burned a torch in a gut I would not take a duck through, and I have a ship and forty casks because of it. I have told that at every table from here to the Rhine and I will tell it at Dorestat till they pay me to stop.
I have no ship. I have nine men, and I have them because this one was lying off that sand when he need not have been. A ship can be built. I have told that at every table from here to the Rhine.

The old king's law says we may not swear together. Good. I do not like oaths, they are for people who cannot remember what they said. It also says we may agree to help each other in shipwreck. So: we agree. Nobody swear anything.

Two pennies a keel each time she clears this river. From the box: half a lost hull made good, bread for the men who get ashore, and a boat with a horn at the bar on thick nights, so that nobody steers by fires at all.
And the strand stays the lord's. We do not touch his custom. We only mean to stop feeding it.
Put two hundred pennies in the box, and your name first on the stick
Put your name on the stick and no silver: you have paid in already
A box does not put a fire out. Not yet

Your silver is the first sound the box makes. Then Liudbrand's, then the Kentishmen's, then a Saxon nobody knew was in the room. Nobody swears; everybody drinks, which the law does not forbid. The woman of the house keeps the box and, since she now answers for it, keeps a corner of her store for your goods as well. Each master cuts his marks for the bar on one long stick, and you are given the copy. And the Frisians of Dorestat, who have had Liudbrand's story at every table for a fortnight, send down nine hundred pennies by his hand: 'for the nine', he says, 'or the forty casks. They did not say which.'

Liudbrand says that is fair and the Kentishman says it is Frisian, and both are right. Your notch is cut first all the same. Each master cuts his marks for the bar on one long stick and you are given the copy. Six hundred pennies come down from Dorestat by Liudbrand's hand, from men who have heard his story once too often to send nothing.
Liudbrand shrugs and says the box will be empty a while longer, then, since nobody wants to be the first fool. He will be at the wic till his hull is tight.
The lord's table

Odalric has sent a horse for you. At his table there is roast heron, and wine that came by sea and paid no toll. Adalwin the steward stands behind his lord's bench with his tally sticks, like a man waiting to be asked a sum.
You bought on my sand and did not run to a priest about it. So I can speak plainly, which I enjoy and seldom get to do.
My strand gives me cloth, lead, wine, wax. I am a soldier. I sell it like a soldier, to the first man with a cart, for a third of its worth. You know what things fetch and where.
Three ships in three winters. Sold as my lord sells, four thousand pennies. Sold properly, by a man with a boat and friends at Dorestat, nearer nine.
A third of what you sell for me, and my hand over you from this river to the next. No toll man on my shore will know your name and every one of my men will.
One thing, said once. A man who eats at this table and afterwards goes to the judges is a man my people will not show the gut to on a thick night. I say it now so that it need never be said again.
Take the third, and his hand over you
Sell this year's for him, once, and take silver and no stick
Thank him for the heron, and say you sell only what was bought

Adalwin splits a stick and you take your half. Nine hundred pennies on account, ten bolts of English cloth to begin with, and a man of Odalric's to show you the gut and the wreck-post and which dune not to look at. The three Englishmen, if they are still in the byre, are sent home at the lord's cost: 'a gift to my partner's conscience'. You are a rich man on this coast and a safe one. On thick nights you will know, wherever you are, what is burning.

Odalric says a careful man is a kind of honest man and he will take what he can get. You sell the winter's cloth and lead for him at the wic and up the Rhine for nearly three times what the carts brought, and keep six hundred and fifty. His hand is over you on that shore for it. Adalwin keeps your name on a stick anyway. He says he keeps everybody's.

He is not offended. He says most men find their price at the second asking and he will not ask a second time. The horse takes you back. What you bought on the sand is still yours, and still has a cross cut in it.

The emperor's judges sat at the wic on the Canche and gave judgement for the abbess of Thanet against the lord of the south strand. No fire is to burn on that shore by night but one, on the hill of Saint Josse, kept by the brothers. A Frisian brought the suit.

The lord of the strand south of the Canche has let three English seamen go without payment and made the abbess of Thanet a gift for her lead. Nobody says the judges made him. The judges were sitting at the wic that week.

Three men of the abbess of Thanet's lost ship are home, bought back off a Frankish sand at fifty pennies a head. Masters bound for the Canche are told: the fire you want is the high one. Do not turn in on a low one.

The shipmasters at the wic on the Canche, Frisian and English, have agreed to help each other in shipwreck: two pennies a keel into a box, half a lost hull made good, and a boat with a horn at the bar on thick nights. Nobody swore to it. The law allows that.
Early morning on the river bank at Quentovic, grey and windy: two fishermen carrying a soaked man on a hatch board, his arm locked round it; behind them the long street and a row of beached boats.
Inside a long alehouse by firelight: an old fisherman at the bench end by the door drawing three lines in spilt ale with one finger, a merchant leaning in, other drinkers carefully looking elsewhere.

Night at sea off a low dune coast under thick cloud: a small boat at anchor in the foreground with two men at the rail, a single low fire on the black shore burning unevenly, and far to the north nothing where a steady light ought to be.

A wide grey strand at low water in morning light: a ship on her side with sprung planks, women and children carrying wet bolts of cloth toward the dunes, an ox cart with grey pigs of lead, and a lean man cutting notches in a stick.

A timber hall behind sea dunes with a new thatch: a well-dressed Frankish lord on a bench with an ale cup, three thin English seamen in borrowed tunics standing in a row by the door, a merchant facing them.

Inside a long oak shed open to a chalk strand: empty rollers on the floor, a tall pale abbess in a dark veil with a staff standing where a ship's stem would be, a small nun with a wax tablet behind her, a merchant with a wet cloak before them.
A cattle byre in low autumn light: three thin men with dung forks, one a coughing boy, a Frankish lord in a good cloak at the door with his thumbs in his belt, a merchant holding a purse.

The sunny south wall of a small guest hall inside a fence, dunes and a hill behind: four weathered English seamen on a bench, one a boy, a tonsured monk standing with a pot, a merchant crouched before them listening.
Night behind boat sheds on a river bank, one rushlight: a bent old man with scarred forearms and a girl of ten holding his sleeve, a merchant facing them, the black river behind.

Black night at sea off a dune shore: a small boat with a flaring pitch torch at her masthead in the foreground, a big deep-laden ship under a reefed square sail looming out of the murk, a dirty orange fire low on the land behind.

Open ground before a small stone church on a bright cold day: an abbot and a count on a bench, a clerk with an open leaf, a Frankish lord with twelve men behind him on one side; on the other a merchant, a huge Frisian shipmaster, four English seamen and a grey pig of lead on the ground.

A chalk strand under a high pale sky: a woman holding a thin boy by the ear, two seamen kneeling to an abbess at the doors of a ship-house with a cross over them, a nun reading from a small charter, a little Frisian boat afloat behind.

A crowded alehouse by firelight: Frisian and English shipmasters shoulder to shoulder at one long table, a huge Frisian with a small empty oak box before him, a long tally stick being notched, a woman with a jug watching from the cask.

A lord's table by torchlight in a timber hall: a roast heron, a silver cup, a well-dressed Frankish lord leaning forward with open hands, a lean steward behind him holding a split tally stick out toward a merchant.
